entry: Process of cooling a space, substance or system to below ambient temperature. Early refrigeration relied on consumable coolants such as ice and dry ice. Modern refrigeration is a self-sustaining process in which a refrigerant absorbs heat from a cold medium and releases it to a warmer one, typically through phase change in a compressor and radiator system. Applications include [[Refrigerator|household refrigerators]], industrial freezers and cryogenics. For most of history, cold storage was possible mainly in arctic and alpine regions, where natural ice could be harvested, while other societies preserved food by curing and drying. Mechanical refrigeration developed in the late 19th and mid-20th centuries, and refrigerated rail cars helped settle [[Houston]], Texas, and [[Las Vegas]], Nevada. Refrigeration now underpins food processing, distribution and retail. Early chlorofluorocarbon refrigerants depleted stratospheric ozone, prompting phase-outs.

Insulated appliance that keeps its interior cold by pumping heat out to the surrounding room. A refrigerator, commonly shortened to fridge, is a commercial and home appliance using a [[Heat pump|heat pump]] that transfers heat from inside to the external environment. The low temperature slows bacterial reproduction and so reduces spoilage. Perishable food is best kept at 3 to 5 °C (37 to 41 °F), and freezers are kept below the freezing point of water. The refrigerator replaced the icebox, a common household appliance for almost a century and a half. The first commercial ice-making machine was invented in 1854, and refrigerators for home use were invented in 1913. In 1923 Frigidaire introduced the first self-contained unit, and home freezers were introduced in 1940, making frozen foods commonplace. Most household refrigerators use a vapor compression cycle.

Person forced to flee their own country. According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), a refugee cannot return home because of feared persecution, armed conflict, violence or serious public disorder. A person may be called an asylum seeker until granted refugee status. Internally displaced people have not crossed an international border, although they may have fled for the same reasons. In Western history the term was first applied to French Protestant Huguenots seeking safety after the first Edict of Fontainebleau in 1540. The 1951 [[United Nations|United Nations]] Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees defined a refugee as someone with a well-founded fear of persecution, a definition confirmed by a 1967 protocol. The Organization of African Unity's 1969 definition extended protection to people fleeing external aggression, occupation or events seriously disturbing public order.

Music genre that originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s. Reggae developed from the earlier Jamaican genres ska and rocksteady and draws on traditional drumming styles and African folk rhythms. It is distinguished by a slower tempo than ska, a strong emphasis on the downbeat, short offbeat guitar or piano chords, and a central bass guitar. Vocals are often in Jamaican Patois, and lyrics address social and political issues, religion and love. Reggae is closely associated with [[Rastafari|Rastafari]], a religion that emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s. The 1968 single "Do the Reggay" by Toots and the Maytals was the first popular song to use the word. From the 1970s, international success spread Rastafarian beliefs, and [[Bob Marley|Bob Marley]]'s 1980 visit to Zimbabwe boosted the genre in Africa.

American football defensive end who played 15 seasons in the [[National Football League|National Football League (NFL)]], mainly with the Philadelphia Eagles and Green Bay Packers. He held second place among NFL career sack leaders, with 198, and was a two-time Defensive Player of the Year, a [[Super Bowl|Super Bowl XXXI]] champion and a 13-time Pro Bowl selection. White is credited with pioneering free agency in sports. An ordained evangelical minister, he was nicknamed the "Minister of Defense." He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

American actress, director and producer. King won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for *If Beale Street Could Talk* (2018) and four Primetime Emmy Awards, for her work in *American Crime*, *Seven Seconds* and *Watchmen*. She first gained attention in the sitcom *227* (1985–1990). She directed episodes of *Scandal* and *This Is Us* and made her feature directing debut with *One Night in Miami...* (2020). In 2019 *Time* magazine named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world.

City (pop., 2021: 226,404), capital of Saskatchewan, Canada. The second-largest city in the province after [[Saskatoon]], Regina is a commercial centre for southern Saskatchewan. The site was called Wascana until 1882, when it was renamed in honor of [[Queen Victoria]]. The federal government made Regina the seat of government for the new province in 1905. The 1912 Regina Cyclone destroyed much of the town. In 1933 the CCF, now the NDP, formulated its Regina Manifesto in the city, and Regina became a center of political activism and the cooperative movement.

Portion of the Earth's surface defined by physical, human or integrated characteristics. Regions, also called areas, zones or territories, often have imprecise and sometimes transitory boundaries, except in human geography, where national borders are defined in law. The largest land and water regions are [[Continent|continents]] and [[Ocean|oceans]]. Physical regions are based on natural features such as [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]], [[Biome|biomes]], [[Drainage basin|drainage basins]] and [[Mountain range|mountain ranges]]. Human regions are described by ethnography. Geographers also distinguish formal regions, which are uniform in measurable traits, from functional regions organized around a central node such as a city. Regional geography studies regions of all sizes and seeks to define the character of each.

Set of statistical methods for estimating the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. The most common form is [[Linear regression|linear regression]], which fits a line or hyperplane to data, usually by [[Ordinary least squares|ordinary least squares]], minimizing the squared differences between observations and the line. Regression is widely used for prediction and forecasting, where it overlaps with [[Machine learning|machine learning]]. It can also suggest causal relationships, but this requires justification, especially with observational data. The earliest form appeared in the work of [[Isaac Newton|Isaac Newton]] in 1700. The method of least squares was published by [[Adrien-Marie Legendre|Legendre]] in 1805 and by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] in 1809. The term "regression" was coined by [[Francis Galton|Francis Galton]] in the 19th century to describe how the heights of descendants of tall ancestors tend to regress toward an average.

Sequence of characters that specifies a pattern for matching text, also called regex or regexp. Regular expressions are used by string-searching algorithms for "find" and "find and replace" operations and for input validation. They appear in [[Search engine|search engines]], text editors, [[Word processor|word processors]] and utilities such as sed and AWK. The concept was formalized by Stephen Cole Kleene in the 1950s as a description of regular languages in [[Formal language|formal language theory]]. Regular expressions entered popular use from 1968, when Ken Thompson built the notation into the QED text editor and later into the Unix editor ed, leading to the grep command.

Brightest star in the constellation Leo, a quadruple star system about 79 light years (24.2 parsecs) from the [[Solar System|Solar System]]. Regulus appears single but is organized into two pairs. Regulus A is a blue-white main-sequence star with a companion, a pre-white dwarf, and Regulus BC is a close pair. Regulus is the 21st-brightest star in the night sky, with an apparent magnitude of +1.35. Its Bayer designation is Alpha Leonis, and its traditional name is Latin for "prince" or "little king." Lying 0.465 degrees from the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]], it is often occulted by the Moon, in spates every 9.3 years.

Period of massacres and public executions during the French Revolution. Historians disagree on when it began, dating it variously from July 1789 to 1793. It responded to Federalist revolts, anticlerical sentiment and accusations of treason by the Committee of Public Safety, although terror was never formally instituted as legal policy. It ended with the fall of [[Maximilien Robespierre|Robespierre]] in July 1794. By then 16,594 official death sentences had been handed down since June 1793, 2,639 of them in Paris. An estimated ten- to twenty thousand more people were executed without trial or died awaiting trial in prison.

Belief that the nonmaterial essence of a living being is reborn in a new body after death. Also called rebirth or transmigration, the concept is a central tenet of Indian religions such as [[Hinduism|Hinduism]], [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], [[Jainism|Jainism]] and [[Sikhism|Sikhism]]. It also appears in some streams of Judaism, in pagan religions including Wicca, and among Indigenous peoples of the Americas and Aboriginal Australians. The ancient Greek thinkers [[Pythagoras|Pythagoras]], [[Socrates|Socrates]] and [[Plato|Plato]] accepted a form of the soul's rebirth called metempsychosis. Some Abrahamic denominations reject reincarnation, while Hasidic Judaism, the Druze and Rastafarians accept it. Indian religions regard rebirth as a cycle to be escaped through liberation, called [[Nirvana|nirvana]] or moksha.

Species of deer (*Rangifer tarandus*), known as caribou in North America. Reindeer have a circumpolar distribution across the [[Arctic|Arctic]], subarctic, tundra, boreal and mountainous regions of Northern Europe, Siberia and North America. They are the only representative of the genus *Rangifer*. Reindeer vary greatly in size, from the smallest, the Svalbard reindeer, to the largest, Osborn's caribou. Unlike other deer, females may have antlers. Reindeer are the only deer successfully semi-domesticated on a large scale, and both wild and domestic animals have long provided food, clothing and shelter for Arctic peoples. In traditional Christmas legends, [[Santa Claus|Santa Claus]]'s reindeer pull his sleigh. Some species and subspecies are in decline and considered vulnerable.

German SS and police official in Nazi Germany and a principal architect of the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. From 1939 he headed the Reich Security Main Office, which included the [[Gestapo|Gestapo]], and he chaired the January 1942 Wannsee Conference on the "Final Solution." He helped organize [[Kristallnacht|Kristallnacht]] and directed the Einsatzgruppen, which murdered more than two million people, including 1.3 million Jews. Czech and Slovak soldiers trained by Britain's Special Operations Executive ambushed him in Prague in May 1942. He died of sepsis from his injuries, and Nazi reprisals destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky.

Indian film actress, primarily of Hindi cinema. Born Bhanurekha Ganesan, she began as a child actress in Telugu films. Her Hindi debut was *Sawan Bhadon* (1970), and she became one of the leading stars of Hindi cinema in the 1980s. She won the National Film Award for Best Actress for *Umrao Jaan* (1981) and three Filmfare Awards, including one for *Khubsoorat* (1980). She received the Padma Shri in 2010 and served in the Rajya Sabha from 2012 to 2018. Her films with [[Amitabh Bachchan|Amitabh Bachchan]] drew enduring media speculation about a romance.

Family of philosophical views that deny absolute objectivity within a domain, holding that valuations depend on an observer or context. Moral relativism holds that moral judgments differ among people and cultures without an absolute standard. Epistemic relativism holds that there are no absolute principles of belief, justification or rationality. Alethic relativism holds that [[Truth|truth]] is always relative to a frame of reference, such as a language or culture, while linguistic relativism holds that a language's structures influence how speakers perceive the world. Anthropologists usually practice descriptive relativism, describing cultural differences without judging them, in order to avoid [[Ethnocentrism|ethnocentrism]]. Critics argue that relativism is self-contradictory and cannot condemn practices in other cultures, while supporters credit it with promoting tolerance.

Branch of physics describing motion and forces at speeds comparable to that of light. Relativistic mechanics is compatible with [[Special relativity|special relativity]] and [[General relativity|general relativity]]. Unlike Galilean relativity, which permitted speeds above that of light, it extends classical mechanics to high velocities and energies and is consistent with electromagnetism. Like classical mechanics, it treats kinematics and dynamics, but it changes the concepts of space, time, mass, momentum and energy. Special relativity shows that mass, momentum and energy are aspects of the same physical quantity. Force remains the time derivative of momentum. Relativistic momentum is p = γmv, where γ is the Lorentz factor, and total energy is E = γmc², which reduces to E = mc² for an object at rest. Combining general relativity with [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] remains an unsolved problem in [[Quantum gravity|quantum gravity]].

Electrically operated switch, used to control a circuit with a separate low-power signal. A relay can also control several circuits with one signal. Relays were first used in long-distance [[Telegraphy|telegraph]] circuits as signal repeaters, transmitting a refreshed copy of an incoming signal. They were used extensively in telephone exchanges and early [[Computer|computers]] for logical operations. The traditional electromechanical relay uses an [[Electromagnet|electromagnet]] to open or close contacts, while solid-state relays use semiconductors with no moving parts. Latching relays need only one pulse to operate and another to reset. Samuel Thomas von Sömmerring designed an electrolytic relay as a telegraph alarm in 1809. An 1840 patent to [[Samuel Morse|Samuel Morse]] described a telegraph repeater that is now called a relay.

Object of religious significance from the past, usually the remains or personal effects of a saint or other holy person. Relics are venerated as tangible memorials and are important in Buddhism, Hinduism, [[Christianity|Christianity]], [[Islam|Islam]] and shamanism. The word derives from Latin *reliquiae*, meaning "remains." A reliquary is a shrine that houses relics. In ancient Greece a city might claim a hero's remains, while weapons, chariots and other objects associated with the hero were displayed. The Delphic Oracle advised the Spartans to find the bones of Orestes before a war. In Christianity, the Catholic Church classifies relics into three types: bodily parts, items touched to a [[Saint|saint]], and objects touched to those relics. Relic cults proliferated from the 4th century, and the Reformation brought iconoclasm and controversy over relics in the 16th century.

Polytheistic religion of ancient Rome, combining state cults, household worship and provincial practices. Roman religion was practical and contractual, based on the reciprocal principle of *do ut des*, and depended on correct ritual rather than faith or dogma. Romans attributed their success to their collective piety (*pietas*) toward the gods. Greek influence introduced the cult of [[Apollo|Apollo]], while augury derived from Etruscan religion. The state priesthoods were held by the elite, and [[Julius Caesar|Julius Caesar]] became pontifex maximus before he was elected consul. Household shrines and neighborhood sacred places dotted the city, and the Vestals tended Rome's sacred hearth for centuries. The triumph, a religious procession, honored [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]]. [[Christianity|Christianity]] became the official state religion in 380.

Predominantly polytheistic religion of the Arabian Peninsula before Islam. Arab polytheism centered on deities and spirits such as the god Hubal and the goddesses al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt, venerated at local shrines such as the [[Kaaba|Kaaba]] in [[Mecca|Mecca]], which was said to contain up to 360 idols. Worship involved pilgrimage, [[Divination|divination]] and ritual [[Sacrifice|sacrifice]]. Christianity and Judaism were also present, especially from the fourth to seventh centuries, and Judaism formed large communities in southern Arabia and the northwestern Hejaz. Under Persian influence, [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] spread to a limited extent. Evidence comes from inscriptions, poetry, Jewish and Greek accounts and Muslim writings, and information is limited. Some recent research suggests that henotheism or monotheism was dominant from the fourth century onward.

Architecture concerned with the design and construction of places of worship and other sacred spaces. Churches, mosques, stupas, synagogues and temples are among the most impressive and permanent buildings humanity has created, and were often the largest buildings in the world before the modern skyscraper. Sacred architecture uses sacred geometry, iconography and religious symbols. Many ancient temples were regarded as dwellings of the gods, and the [[Temple|Temple]] of Karnak at Thebes, Egypt, was built over 1,300 years and may be the largest religious structure ever built. Around 600 BCE the wooden columns of the Temple of Hera at Olympia were replaced by stone, and most surviving classical architecture is religious. The [[Parthenon|Parthenon]], which also served as a treasury, is widely regarded as the greatest example of classical architecture.

Visual representation of religious ideologies and their relationship with humans. Sacred art is made for worship and religious practice. A cult image is the main image in a place of worship, while a devotional image is a smaller work for private prayer. Opposition to images, called aniconism, has been widespread, and [[Iconoclasm|iconoclasm]] is the deliberate destruction of images by members of the same religion. Buddhist art originated in India after the life of Siddhartha Gautama and spread north through Central Asia and east to Southeast Asia. Tibetan Buddhist art, tied to [[Vajrayana|Vajrayana]] practice, includes thangkas and mandalas made as aids to meditation. Cave paintings at Ajanta, discovered in 1817, and at Dunhuang on the [[Silk Road|Silk Road]] date from about the 5th century AD. Christian art often depicts Jesus and scenes from the Old Testament, while images of the Virgin Mary and saints are much rarer in Protestant art than in Roman Catholic art.

Adoption of the beliefs of one religious denomination to the exclusion of others. Conversion may occur between denominations of the same religion, such as from Shi'a to Sunni Islam, or between religions. People convert for many reasons, including free choice, marriage, convenience and force, and historically to evade taxes, escape military service or gain political representation. *Proselytism* is the attempt to convert others by persuasion. In an 1873 lecture, Max Müller divided religions into missionary religions, such as [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], [[Christianity|Christianity]] and [[Islam|Islam]], which seek converts, and non-missionary religions, such as [[Judaism|Judaism]], [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] and [[Hinduism|Hinduism]]. Someone who has left a religion may be called an [[Apostasy|apostate]].
